strengths: The paper targets two genuinely under-served problems in gloss-free SLT: fingerspelling and asynchronous non-manual (mouth) cues, and the motivation is well argued with linguistic support.

The proposed modular design — specialized predictors for continuous signing, fingerspelling, and lipreading, fused by a transformer before LLM decoding — is sensible and the qualitative examples in the supplementary show the router correctly isolating fingerspelled names.
Reported results are strong: new best BLEU-4 on How2Sign (23.5 vs 15.5 prior best) and best letter accuracy on ChicagoFSWildPlus (73.2% vs 71.1%).

The ablation studies are more thorough than typical: component removal, LLM size sweep, pseudo-glossing strategy comparison, and temporal alignment sensitivity, which together support the paper's core hypothesis about modality-specific experts and alignment.
Temporal-shift ablation (Table 6) directly quantifies the claimed temporal misalignment problem, which strengthens the scientific case for learned alignment over naive frame-wise fusion.
weaknesses: Fairness of comparisons is questionable. Table 1 mixes pose-based and RGB-based baselines with different training data and evaluation protocols, and no baseline is re-run under identical conditions. The jump from 15.5 to 23.5 BLEU-4 is unusually large and demands stronger validation (e.g., identical text preprocessing, same splits, significance testing), especially given the paper's own ablation showing pseudo-glossing strategy alone moves BLEU-4 from 9.6 to 23.5.
Pre-training on YouTube-ASL and evaluating on How2Sign raises potential train/test contamination concerns (How2Sign source videos may appear in YouTube-ASL); this is not discussed or checked.

The method description contains ambiguities and internal inconsistencies: the Gumbel-Softmax sequence classifier is described as making a per-sequence choice, yet Eq. 9 applies per-token gating weights; how 'rest' segments are handled at inference, the fusion transformer's size, and how the router handles mixed sign+fingerspelling within a clip are unclear. The stated 99.2% sequence classification accuracy is reported without specifying the evaluation set or protocol.

Citation and presentation errors undermine confidence: Figure 1's caption describes only the lipreading pipeline (apparently text carried over from another paper) and contains a wrong attribution ('(Vaswani et al. 2017) (Llama)'); the ViT-base backbone is cited to an unrelated autonomous-driving paper (Serdyuk et al. 2022); Graves et al. 2006 appears twice as 2006a/2006b; Shi et al. 2019 is duplicated with different author lists; the How2Sign description contains an obvious typo ('35,19135,191' clips) and an incorrect '8080 hours' figure.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or model release is mentioned, hyperparameters (learning rates, stages' epochs, fusion dimension D, number of layers L), CTC vocabulary construction, and the exact pseudo-glossing procedure for How2Sign labels are unspecified.

Novelty relative to closely related multi-stream work is under-argued: SignMusketeers (Gueuwou et al. 2024) is cited as a multi-stream SLT method but the paper does not clearly delineate what is new beyond adding a fingerspelling expert and Gumbel routing.
Writing quality issues throughout (e.g., 'Continuos', 'dispite', inconsistent ablation numbers: text says 58.9% where Table 3 says 58.8%) suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.
No limitations or societal-impact discussion; error analysis is limited to a few qualitative examples, with no breakdown of performance on fingerspelled vs signed content within full SLT.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and well-motivated gap in gloss-free SLT: fingerspelling and non-manual (lip) cues are indeed under-served by monolithic end-to-end models, and the introduction/related work articulate the temporal-blurring, visual-ambiguity, and data-imbalance challenges clearly.

The modular design (specialized predictors for continuous signing, fingerspelling, and lipreading, combined via a gated fusion transformer before LLM decoding) is sensible and the staged training recipe is described at a level that makes the overall idea easy to grasp.

The evaluation covers two complementary benchmarks (How2Sign for translation, ChicagoFSWild+ for fingerspelling) and includes several ablations (component removal, LLM size, glossing strategies, temporal-shift sensitivity), which is more analysis than many SLT papers provide; the temporal-shift experiment (Table 6) is a nice direct probe of the asynchronicity claim.
Reported numbers, if accurate, are strong: BLEU-4 of 23.5 on How2Sign and 73.2% letter accuracy on ChicagoFSWild+ exceed prior published results.
weaknesses: The core scientific claim — that isolating recognition subtasks before fusion beats a monolithic model — is never tested against the appropriate baseline. The closest ablation ('Without LLM') removes sentence generation, not modularity. A single-branch DINOv2+CTC+LLM model trained on the same data with the same budget is the essential control, and it is missing. Without it, the impressive gains cannot be attributed to the proposed multi-stream hypothesis.

Critical supervision details are unexplained, undermining reproducibility: how are sequence-type (sign/fingerspelling/rest) ground-truth labels obtained for training the Gumbel-Softmax router on How2Sign/YouTube-ASL, which have no such annotations? How is the lipreading branch's phoneme CTC supervised, given that none of the datasets provide phoneme transcriptions? The 99.2% sequence-classification accuracy is reported without any description of how it was measured or on what label source, and it is implausibly high for in-the-wild signing.

The evaluation protocol is ambiguous and raises leakage concerns. The model is pre-trained on YouTube-ASL and ChicagoFSWild+ and then fine-tuned and evaluated on How2Sign; the overlap between these corpora (e.g., fingerspelling data drawn from YouTube sources) and the exact train/val/test splits, decoding setup, and whether prior work used comparable data are not specified. Given a +8 BLEU-4 jump over SSVP-SLT, this needs much tighter justification.

The method section contains inconsistencies and errors that suggest insufficient care: Figure 1's caption describes only the lipreading branch (16 frames, 50% patch masking, phoneme CTC, CMU-dict LLM fine-tuning) rather than the full architecture; the fusion-CTC vocabulary that must mix sign tokens, letters, and phonemes into one target sequence is never defined; Table 3 reports '58.8' while the text says '58.9'; Eq. 5 has mismatched notation; duplicate identical references (Graves et al. 2006a/b); ViT-base is cited to Serdyuk et al. 2022 (an unrelated autonomous-driving paper) instead of Dosovitskiy et al.; '(Vaswani et al. 2017) (Llama (Touvron et al. 2023))' conflates two different works; numerous typos ('Continuos', 'dispite', 'vers', '35,19135,191').

Ablation tables mix datasets without clarification: Table 3 reports Letter Accuracy (a ChicagoFSWild+ metric) alongside BLEU-4 (a How2Sign metric) in one table, with no statement of which dataset each column refers to for each variant, making the component contributions hard to interpret.

Novelty is incremental relative to existing multi-stream SLT work (e.g., SignMusketeers, Koller et al.'s multi-stream CNN-LSTM-HMMs): the components (DINOv2 backbone, CTC heads, sigmoid gating, frozen-then-finetune LLM) are all standard; the contribution reduces to routing fingerspelling vs. continuous signing plus lip fusion, and the gating/asynchronicity machinery (Eqs. 9-11) is generic.

The 'Glossing Methods' ablation is conceptually confused: pseudo-glossing selects content words from the ground-truth sentence as CTC targets. This is simply label preprocessing, yet it is presented as a methodological contribution with an LLM in the loop; the paper does not clarify whether this leaks reference text into the inference-time token vocabulary or how it compares to standard gloss-free training targets.

No reproducibility support: no code release, no hyperparameters, compute budget, training durations, or seeds/variance estimates, which is particularly problematic given the unusually large claimed margins.

No limitations discussion and no societal/ethical considerations, despite the work targeting assistive technology for the Deaf community and relying on YouTube-sourced data of real signers, where consent and privacy are recognized concerns in this field.

strengths: The paper targets a real and under-addressed problem in gloss-free SLT: fingerspelling and asynchronous non-manual cues are plausibly identified as failure modes of monolithic end-to-end models, and the motivation is well grounded in the sign-linguistics literature.

The modular multi-expert design (dedicated fingerspelling, continuous signing, and lipreading predictors with a fusion transformer feeding an LLM) is a sensible and clearly articulated architecture, and the staged training recipe is described at a level that supports reproduction of the overall pipeline.

The ablation studies are reasonably comprehensive: component removal (Table 3), LLM scale (Table 4), pseudo-glossing strategies (Table 5), and explicit temporal-shift experiments for manual/non-manual misalignment (Table 6) provide useful evidence about which parts of the system matter.

Strong reported results on both How2Sign (BLEU-4 23.5) and ChicagoFSWildPlus (73.2% letter accuracy), with a large improvement over prior fingerspelling systems, plus qualitative examples and visualizations in the supplementary material that illustrate dynamic modality routing.

The temporal-shift ablation (Table 6) directly tests the paper's central claim about asynchronicity and shows learned alignment substantially outperforms fixed fusions, which is a valuable empirical finding.
weaknesses: A potentially serious confound undermines the core claim: the lipreading stream on How2Sign may effectively reconstruct the English translation from mouthing alone, since interpreters typically mouth the spoken words. BLEU-4 dropping only from 23.5 to 16.6 without lipreading, and the near-perfect 99.2% sequence-classification accuracy, suggest the system may largely be doing lipreading-plus-language-modeling rather than sign language translation. The paper frames lip cues as 'disambiguating' signals but provides no experiment isolating sign-video-only performance or controlling for mouthing.

Fairness of comparisons is questionable. Table 1 mixes pose-only and RGB baselines, and it is unclear whether baselines used YouTube-ASL pretraining or comparable backbones (DINOv2, ViT, Llama-2-7B). The jump from 15.5 (SSVP-SLT) to 23.5 BLEU-4 is large and could partly reflect backbone/LLM capacity rather than the multi-stream design; no controlled comparison with an equal-capacity single-stream baseline is provided. The ChicagoFSWildPlus comparison similarly pits RGB+lip against pose-based methods.

The claimed mechanism is not well matched to the architecture: the fusion module (Eqs. 9-11) is a simple weighted sum with a sigmoid gate; nothing in it explicitly models temporal misalignment, and the learned-alignment result in Table 6 is not explained mechanistically. The text overstates this as 'explicitly handles temporal asynchronicity.'

Reproducibility is poor: no training hyperparameters, epoch counts, learning rates, hardware, or compute budget; no variance/significance reporting for the headline numbers; and key details (e.g., how the hard Gumbel-Softmax selection behaves at inference, how phoneme sequences from CTC are tokenized for the LLM) are underspecified.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness reduce confidence: Figure 1's caption describes a seemingly different lipreading-only pipeline (16 frames, phoneme reconstruction from a text-only dataset) and awkwardly cites '(Vaswani et al. 2017) (Llama...)' as if Vaswani were Llama; Table 3 text says 58.9% while the table says 58.8%; How2Sign is described as 'over 8080 hours' (incorrect); typos such as 'Continuos,' 'dispite,' and 'vers' appear throughout; the abstract claims evaluation on YouTube-ASL but no YouTube-ASL results table exists.

The pseudo-glossing preprocessing modifies labels using an LLM with knowledge of ASL sentence structure (Table 5, 'LLM Glossing'); this borders on gloss supervision, sits awkwardly with the 'gloss-free' claim, and its interaction with the translation targets deserves more careful justification.

No limitations section, no discussion of societal impact (important for a Deaf-accessibility technology), and no error analysis beyond two cherry-picked supplementary examples; generalization to other sign languages (BSL, DGS) mentioned in the introduction is never tested.

Contribution type: although not declared, this is Algorithms/General; under that lens the novelty is moderate (mixture-of-experts over visual streams plus an LLM head are established patterns), so the contribution rests heavily on empirical evidence, which as noted above has comparability and confound problems.

strengths: The core idea—decomposing SLT into specialized expert streams (continuous signing, fingerspelling, lipreading) with explicit handling of temporal asynchrony before fusion—is well-motivated and addresses genuine, documented weaknesses of single-network gloss-free SLT approaches.
Strong empirical results: new state-of-the-art on three benchmarks (How2Sign BLEU-4 22.1, BOBSL BLEU-4 6.8, ChicagoFSWild+ 73.2% letter accuracy), with large margins over prior end-to-end methods.

Comprehensive ablations: component removal (Table 4), fusion strategy comparison (concatenation vs. cross-attention vs. gated fusion, Table 8), LLM scale (Table 6), and a dedicated temporal-shift study of manual/non-manual alignment (Table 7) that directly probes the paper's central hypothesis.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough: full pseudo-glossing prompts, phonemization pipeline, hyperparameters, parameter counts (Table 13), computational cost, qualitative translations with per-stream outputs, and an insightful POS analysis that candidly discusses weaknesses (e.g., over-reliance on LLM priors for interjections).
Zero-shot transfer experiments from YouTube-ASL to How2Sign (Table 9) support the claim that in-the-wild pre-training provides generalizable representations.
weaknesses: The pipeline is heavily dependent on GPT-4o-generated pseudo-gloss targets, yet the quality/validity of these targets is never evaluated (no human or quantitative assessment of whether the generated glosses resemble actual ASL/BSL production). The system is effectively distilled from an LLM's idea of sign language, which undermines the linguistic claims and the 'gloss-free' framing—a supervised intermediate gloss representation is still being used, just an automatically generated one.

Fairness of SOTA comparisons is questionable. Table 13 shows the model uses a 6.7B-parameter LLM (LLaMA-2-7B) plus a 197.5M visual encoder, while most baselines use mT5-Base or mBart (~580-680M). Part of the +6.6 BLEU-4 gain on How2Sign may come from language-model scale rather than the proposed fusion paradigm; no experiment controls for this (Table 6 varies the LLM only within the proposed system).

The ablations reveal that lipreading is the dominant modality ('W/o Lipreading' B-4 drops from 22.1 to 13.6, and the sign branch alone achieves only 6.3 B-4). Since How2Sign interpreters mouth English words, the model may largely be doing visual speech recognition of spoken English rather than sign language translation. This alternative interpretation is not discussed or controlled for, which affects how the results should be interpreted.

Internal inconsistencies reduce confidence: the text reports 'approximately 108 GPU-hours (10 days)' while Table 16 totals 240 hours; Table 14 lists 100 lipreading epochs while the text says 50; Table 6 evaluates Llama-3.2 variants while the main model is LLaMA-2-7B; the main text says the LLM 'remains frozen' during fine-tuning Phase 2 while Section D.3.3 describes LoRA fine-tuning; Table 7's variant list numbering ('four different temporal shifts') does not match the five table rows and inconsistent ±3/±5 frame definitions.

Metric reporting in Table 4 mixes datasets confusingly: letter accuracy (a ChicagoFSWild+ metric) and BLEU-4 (a How2Sign metric) are placed in one table without stating which dataset each ablation was run on, making the component analysis hard to interpret (e.g., why removing fingerspelling drops letter accuracy to 33.7%).

Overstated novelty claims: 'The first sign language LLM' ignores prior LLM-based SLT systems (Sign2GPT, SignLLM, FLa-LLM, GFSLT-VLP) that the paper itself cites; the qualified novelty (first to combine the three streams) should be the claim throughout.

Practicality concerns are acknowledged but severe: ~240 GPU-hours training, 78GB peak memory, and 30-60 minutes for inference on the How2Sign test set on an RTX 4090; no distillation or efficiency results are provided.

No code or data release is mentioned, and the reliance on GPT-4o-generated pseudo-glosses would make exact reproduction difficult even with code; this is significant given the pseudo-gloss prompt is described as 'critical' to performance.
Writing quality needs attention (e.g., 'dicussed', 'aslo', 'psuedo', 'Fingerpelling'), and a limitations discussion appears only in the supplementary rather than the main paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and underexplored problem in gloss-free SLT: fingerspelling and non-manual (lip) cues are indeed neglected by prior end-to-end systems, and the modular decomposition into specialized experts is a sensible and well-motivated design.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough: prompts for pseudo-gloss generation, full hyperparameters, LoRA configuration, computational costs, and parameter-count comparisons against baselines are all provided, which supports reproducibility.

A reasonably broad ablation suite is presented (component removals, LLM scaling, fusion strategy comparison, temporal-shift sensitivity, zero-shot transfer, and a POS-level error analysis), and the authors are candid about failure modes such as proper-noun hallucination and semantic drift, as well as the INTJ-category artifact of LLM priors.

The POS analysis in the supplement is a genuinely interesting diagnostic that goes beyond aggregate BLEU and reveals a concrete trade-off (strong content-word recognition, weak function-word generation).
weaknesses: Severe confound in the headline claim: the model uses a 7B LLaMA decoder and GPT-4o-generated pseudo-gloss/phoneme targets, while most compared baselines use mT5/mBart (~580-680M LM parameters) and weaker supervision. The claimed +6.6 BLEU-4 on How2Sign cannot be attributed to the proposed fusion architecture; the parameter table (Table 13) makes the imbalance explicit but no controlled experiment isolates the architecture contribution from the LM scale. An apples-to-apples baseline (same LLaMA-7B decoder, same pseudo-gloss targets, single stream) is missing.

A critical unresolved question: is this a sign language translation system or largely a lipreading system? Table 5 shows the continuous sign branch alone achieves only 6.3 BLEU-4, and the text states lipreading 'delivers most of the performance improvement.' Crucially, no full-pipeline ablation with lipreading alone is reported. Since the lipreading supervision is phonemized from the English subtitles, and mouthed English is present throughout, the pipeline risks degenerating into visual speech recognition + LLM text generation, which would substantially weaken the contribution's framing.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results: (a) Table 8 shows cross-attention fusion slightly outperforming gated fusion (22.3 vs 22.1), yet the caption and text claim the gated approach is not matched and is preferable — the narrative contradicts the numbers; (b) the 'W/o Fingerspelling' ablation reports letter accuracy dropping from 73.2 to 33.7, but 73.2 is the ChicagoFSWildPlus fingerspelling score while other ablation rows report How2Sign metrics, and the mapping between rows and evaluation protocols is never clarified; (c) Table 7 describes '±5 frames' shifts as 't±3 frames' in the body text; (d) the 'W/o Sequencer' variant references a 'Sequencer' component that is not clearly defined.

The 'Asynchronicity-Aware Fusion Encoder' is oversold. The mechanism is a simple linear+sigmoid gate over concatenated features, and the 'learned alignment' in Table 7 is not described as any explicit temporal alignment mechanism — the gate has no natural way to shift lip features relative to hand features, so the central novelty claim (resolving temporal asynchrony) is not convincingly substantiated by the architecture as described.

Overclaiming and citation problems: the abstract and Figure 1 claim 'the first sign language LLM,' ignoring Sign2GPT, SignLLM, and other LLM-based SLT works the paper itself cites; GPT-4o is cited via reference [47], which is Radford's GPT-1 paper. The paper also reports it was trained with ASL prompts and applied to BSL with a trivially adapted prompt, yet claims effective cross-language generalization without analysis.

The ChicagoFSWildPlus comparison (Table 3) lacks protocol details: it is unclear whether the fingerspelling expert is evaluated in isolation or as part of the full pipeline, whether the compared methods use the same input resolution/cropping, and why several rows (e.g., CtoML) are not ordered consistently. A 2.1-point gain over FS PoseNet on a fingerspelling-specific benchmark with a much larger shared backbone (DINOv2 101M) is not strong evidence of architectural advantage.

Writing quality is below venue standard: numerous typos ('psuedo-glosses', 'It aslo', 'Fingerpelling', 'sing-aligned'), broken sentences (Section 3.4 'to get a sequence-level representation, A small MLP'), and the 'Fu' orphaned text on page 2. For a paper whose claims rest on subtle ablation interpretation, this sloppiness matters.

No significant-variation analysis, no statistical tests, and BOBSL evaluation uses only a small subset of baselines, some of which are weak (B4 0.6-2.6), making the +4.2 improvement claim hard to contextualize.

strengths: The paper targets two well-motivated, genuinely under-served problems in gloss-free SLT: fingerspelling recognition and integration of non-manual (mouth) cues with their temporal asynchrony, supported by relevant sign-linguistics literature.
Strong empirical results: new state-of-the-art on three benchmarks (How2Sign BLEU-4 22.1, BOBSL BLEU-4 6.8, ChicagoFSWildPlus 73.2% letter accuracy), with large margins over prior work.

Unusually thorough ablation suite: component ablations (Table 4), per-modality stand-alone performance (Table 5), LLM scale (Table 6), temporal shift sensitivity (Table 7), fusion strategy comparison (Table 8), pre-training/zero-shot transfer (Table 9), and a fine-grained POS-level linguistic analysis that honestly discusses weaknesses (function words, interjection overfitting).

Comprehensive supplementary material with prompts, hyperparameters, parameter accounting, computational cost, and extensive qualitative examples including failure modes (proper-noun hallucination, semantic drift), which supports reproducibility and transparent error analysis.
The staged training curriculum (frozen experts -> fusion -> LLM) is well documented and the modular design is sensible and clearly presented.
weaknesses: Scientific interpretation concern: the stand-alone ablations show the continuous sign branch alone achieves only BLEU-4 6.3, while lipreading contributes most of the gain (65.6% phoneme accuracy; w/o lipreading drops to 13.6 B-4). Much of the reported improvement may come from reading mouthed English (especially on BOBSL, where interpreters mouth English words) rather than from sign recognition per se. The paper partially acknowledges this but should analyze it more explicitly, since it qualifies the central claim that multi-stream fusion is the path to better SLT.

The fingerspelling contribution appears weaker than claimed: in the qualitative tables (17/18) the fingerspelling stream is empty in nearly all examples, and removing it degrades letter accuracy dramatically (33.7%) but B-4 only from 22.1 to 18.9. The core narrative (fingerspelling as a first-class modality driving SOTA) is not fully supported by the evidence presented.

No baseline isolating the value of pseudo-gloss supervision: it is unclear how much of the gain comes from GPT-4o-generated pseudo-gloss targets vs. the multi-stream architecture itself, and pseudo-gloss quality is never quantified (e.g., against human glosses). Given GPT-4o is central to target generation, reproducibility and quality of these labels deserve analysis.

Fairness of comparisons: the system uses a 7B LLaMA-2 decoder plus YouTube-ASL pre-training, whereas many baselines use mT5/mBart; although Table 13 reports parameter counts, the BLEU gains are partly attributable to LLM scale rather than the proposed architecture.

Internal inconsistencies that should be fixed: text states ~108 GPU-hours total training while Table 16 sums to 240 hours; Table 7 lists 'Δ±10 frames: fuse frame t of hands with lip t±5 frames'; Table 6 describes 'fully fine-tuned' LLMs while Section D.3.3 states LLaMA-2-7B is LoRA-adapted with frozen base; Table 9 attributes How2Sign results to 'Alvarez et al. [11]' whose reference is Duarte et al. Also the symbol G is reused (pseudo-gloss sequence in Eq. 2 and Conv1D output in Eq. 9), and stray text fragments ('Fu-', 'nuance') appear in the main text.

The adaptive gating (Eq. 12) dimensions and mechanism are under-specified (is α per-frame, per-batch?), and the router supervises only segments as {Sign, Fingerspelling, Rest} — how these segment labels are obtained is not clearly described.

Evaluation on ChicagoFSWildPlus mixes a fingerspelling-only metric (letter accuracy) with an SLT pipeline; the evaluation protocol (train/test splits, use of extra data vs. prior fingerspelling-specific methods) should be clarified to ensure comparability.
